text: One day a young Italian who had been selling penny ices from a small green handcart appeared at my door, and though he spoke hardly a word of English, I took him on as both servant and model. <break time="0.8s" /> His name was Oronte, and before long this cheerful seller of ices, dressed in borrowed English clothes, was posing as the hero of Rutland Ramsay, and looking every inch a gentleman. <break time="0.8s" /> The Major, finding his place taken by a former street seller, asked me with forced lightness whether this was my idea of an English gentleman, and I could see how deeply the question hurt him. <break time="0.8s" /> To be placed below a servant and a cockney girl was a humiliation that no one of their class could have imagined, yet they bore it in silence, still hoping that their turn would come. <break time="0.8s" /> Then my friend Jack Hawley, a painter whose judgment I trusted, returned from abroad, and, looking over the Rutland Ramsay drawings with a fresh eye, he declared that the work was simply bad. <break time="0.8s" /> They will not do, he said of the Monarchs, warning me in his blunt way that I must get back into my boat at once or I would go straight to the bottom. <break time="0.8s" /> The warning was serious, for the publishers had also begun to doubt my drawings, and my share in the rest of the series was to depend entirely on the satisfaction I should give with the first book. <break time="0.8s" /> I knew that Hawley was right, and yet so much did I pity the Monarchs that, for a while longer, I kept them on, giving them the minor parts and telling myself that they might still improve.
